plain_explanation: If you leave your job, you promise not to work for or start a competing business anywhere in India for the next 12 months. This restriction applies to any business that competes with your current employer.
legal_assessment: This clause is a post-employment non-compete agreement. Under Indian law, agreements that prevent a person from exercising a lawful profession or business after their employment ends are generally void and unenforceable. While restrictions during active employment are valid, this specific 12-month post-termination ban is likely illegal.
recommended_action: Ask to remove this clause entirely, as it is likely unenforceable. If the company insists on keeping it, consult a lawyer to understand the specific risks, but be aware that Indian courts typically strike down such post-employment restraints.
consequence: the clause is likely unenforceable, but the company could still try to use it to threaten you or stop you from finding new work

cited_sources.text:
Agreement in restraint of trade, void.—Every agreement by which any one is restrained from
exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void.
_Exception_ 1.—Saving of agreement not to carry on business of which good-will is sold.—One
who sells the good-will of a business may agree with the buyer to refrain from carrying on a similar business, within specified local limits, so long as the buyer, or any person deriving title to the good-will from him, carries on a like business therein, provided that such limits appear to the Court reasonable, regard being had to the nature of the business.

plain_explanation: While you work for this company, you must give all your working hours to them. You are not allowed to do any other paid work or business activities on the side.
legal_assessment: This clause restricts the employee's activities only during the period of active employment. Under Indian law, agreements that prevent an employee from engaging in other business while they are employed are generally valid and enforceable, as they do not restrain trade after the employment ends. Therefore, this is a standard exclusivity clause.
recommended_action: Nothing to do; this is a standard term for full-time employment.

withheld_claims.claim: Restrictions on an employee's ability to engage in other commercial activities during the term of active employment are valid and not void under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.

plain_explanation: You will be paid a monthly salary of Rs 50,000. The payment will be made on the last working day of each month. The money will be sent directly to the bank account you have provided.
legal_assessment: This is a standard factual clause stating the amount and method of payment. No specific legal question arises from this text alone, and no relevant statutory sections were retrieved to analyze further.
recommended_action: Nothing to do; this is standard. Just make sure the bank account details you provide are correct.

plain_explanation: If you quit your job without working out your full notice period, you must pay the company an amount equal to six months of your total gross salary.
legal_assessment: This clause stipulates a fixed sum (six months' gross salary) as liquidated damages for leaving early. Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, if a contract names a sum to be paid in case of breach, the court will only award reasonable compensation not exceeding that amount, provided it is not a penalty. A sum equal to six months' salary for a notice period breach is likely to be considered an exorbitant penalty rather than a genuine pre-estimate of loss, making the clause potentially unenforceable to that extent. The company can only claim actual reasonable damages, which are typically much lower than six months' pay.
recommended_action: Negotiate to reduce this amount to a reasonable estimate of the company's actual loss, such as the cost of hiring a replacement or the salary for the specific notice period not served, rather than a fixed six-month sum.
consequence: you could be sued for a large sum that a court might still reduce, but you will face significant legal costs and stress trying to prove the amount is unreasonable

cited_sources.text:
Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for.—[1][When a contract has
been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
_Explanation.—A stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a stipulation by_
way of penalty.]
_Exception.—When any person enters into any bail-bond, recognizance or other instrument of the_
same nature, or, under the provisions of any law, or under the orders of the [2][Central Government] or of any [3][State Government], gives any bond for the performance of any public duty or act in which the public are interested, he shall be liable, upon breach of the condition of any such instrument, to pay the whole sum mentioned therein.
_Explanation.—A person who enters into a contract with Government does not necessarily thereby_
undertake any public duty, or promise to do an act in which the public are interested.
_Illustrations_

is entitled to recover from A such compensation, not exceeding Rs. 1,000, as the Court considers reasonable.

Calcutta. B is entitled to such compensation; not exceeding Rs. 5,000, as the Court considers reasonable.
(c)A gives a recognizance binding him in a penalty of Rs. 500 to appear in Court on a certain day. He forfeits his
recognizance. He is liable to pay the whole penalty.

plain_explanation: If you break a company rule, your boss can take half of your monthly pay as a fine. This money is deducted from the wages you have already earned.
legal_assessment: This clause allows the employer to withhold 50% of your earned wages as a penalty for disciplinary violations. Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a party cannot recover a sum that operates as a penalty rather than a genuine pre-estimate of loss. A flat 50% deduction from earned wages is likely an unlawful penalty because it is not tied to the actual financial loss suffered by the employer. Furthermore, withholding a significant portion of earned wages for disciplinary reasons is generally considered an unfair deduction and may violate labor laws protecting wages.
recommended_action: Remove this clause entirely or replace it with a provision that states any deductions will be based on actual, documented losses and will not exceed a reasonable amount. Do not sign the contract with this 50% deduction clause included.
consequence: you could lose half of your monthly salary for a minor rule violation

claims.claim: A stipulation for a fixed sum (like 50% of wages) that is not a genuine pre-estimate of loss operates as a penalty, and the court will only award reasonable compensation not exceeding that amount, effectively invalidating the automatic 50% deduction as a penalty.

plain_explanation: You agree to pay for any losses, claims, or damages the company suffers if they are caused directly by your gross negligence or willful misconduct. This means you are personally responsible for covering these specific costs if you act carelessly or intentionally do something wrong.
legal_assessment: This clause creates a contract of indemnity, which is a legal arrangement where one party promises to save the other from loss. Under Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, such contracts are valid and enforceable. However, because this clause shifts financial liability for losses directly onto you as the employee, it requires careful scrutiny to ensure the scope of 'gross negligence' and 'willful misconduct' is clearly defined and that the potential liability is not excessive or one-sided.
recommended_action: Ask the company to define what constitutes 'gross negligence' and 'willful misconduct' in the contract to avoid vague interpretations. Consider consulting a lawyer to review the clause to ensure the financial liability is reasonable and limited to direct losses.
consequence: you could be personally liable for significant financial losses if the company claims your actions were grossly negligent or willful

claims.claim: The clause constitutes a contract of indemnity, which is legally defined as a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor or any other person.

cited_sources.title: “Contract of indemnity” defined
cited_sources.text:
“Contract of indemnity” defined.—A contract by which one party promises to save the other
from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself, or by the conduct of any other person, is called a “contract of indemnity”.
_Illustration_
A contracts to indemnify B against the consequences of any proceedings which C may take against B in respect of a certain
sum of 200 rupees. This is a contract of indemnity.

plain_explanation: Either you or your employer can end this job contract by giving 30 days' written notice. If you do not want to wait the full 30 days, you can pay your basic salary for that period instead.
legal_assessment: This is a standard mutual termination clause. It allows both parties to end the employment relationship on equal terms with a reasonable notice period or payment in lieu of notice. There is no asymmetry or unlawful restraint here, and it aligns with standard employment practices.
recommended_action: Nothing to do; this is a standard and balanced clause.

plain_explanation: Your employer can fire you right away without giving you any warning or notice. However, if you want to quit, you must give them 90 days' notice before you leave.
legal_assessment: This clause creates a grossly asymmetric termination right. While employers have broad discretion to terminate for cause, requiring an employee to give 90 days' notice while allowing the employer to terminate immediately without notice is highly one-sided. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, conditions of service including termination procedures are governed by certified standing orders, which generally require mutual notice periods or specific procedural safeguards to ensure fairness. A clause that strips the employee of any notice period while imposing a long notice period on the employee is likely to be viewed as unfair and potentially unenforceable in its entirety or in part, as it violates the principle of mutuality in service conditions.
recommended_action: Negotiate to make the notice period mutual, such as 30 days for both parties, or ensure that the immediate termination right is strictly limited to cases of gross misconduct with a clear definition. Do not sign this clause as it is.
consequence: you could be fired instantly without any warning or time to find a new job, while you are stuck for 3 months if you want to leave

plain_explanation: You have agreed to work for the company for at least two years because they are providing you with initial training. If you quit before the two years are up, you must pay the company a fixed fee of 300,000 rupees.
legal_assessment: This clause imposes a fixed penalty of INR 3,00,000 for leaving the job early. Under Indian law, a contract cannot enforce a fixed sum as a penalty for breach; the court will only award reasonable compensation for the actual loss suffered by the company. Since this clause demands a specific, high amount regardless of the company's actual loss (such as the cost of training), it is likely unenforceable as a penalty.
recommended_action: Negotiate to replace the fixed fee with a clause that only requires you to reimburse the actual, documented costs of the training if you leave early. Alternatively, ask for a pro-rata refund of training costs based on how long you stayed.
consequence: you could be sued for 300,000 rupees even if the company's actual training costs were much lower

plain_explanation: You will be on a trial period for the first three months of your job. During this time, either you or your employer can end the employment by giving 7 days' written notice.
legal_assessment: This is a standard probation clause. It allows either party to terminate the employment with a short notice period (7 days) during the initial three-month period. This is a common and balanced term in Indian employment contracts that does not appear to violate statutory requirements for notice or termination during probation.
recommended_action: Nothing to do; this is standard.

plain_explanation: You must keep the company's trade secrets, customer data, and source code secret. This duty to keep these things private starts while you work there and continues forever after you leave.
legal_assessment: The clause imposes a confidentiality obligation that lasts 'perpetually' after employment ends. Under Indian law, agreements that restrain a person from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or business after the termination of the contract are generally void. While protecting trade secrets is valid, an indefinite restriction on using or disclosing information that could be considered part of the employee's general skill or knowledge may be viewed as an unlawful restraint of trade. The lack of a time limit makes this clause potentially unenforceable in its entirety or to the extent it restricts post-employment activity.
recommended_action: Ask to limit the confidentiality period to a reasonable time after leaving (for example, 1 to 2 years) and clarify that it only applies to specific trade secrets, not general knowledge or skills.
consequence: the company could claim you are breaking the contract for using your own skills or knowledge after you leave, even if the clause is legally weak

plain_explanation: For one year after you leave the company, you are not allowed to ask the company's current clients to do business with you or others. You are also not allowed to encourage the company's current employees to quit their jobs.
legal_assessment: This clause imposes a non-solicitation restriction that continues for 12 months after your employment ends. Under Indian law, agreements that restrain a person from exercising a lawful profession or trade after the termination of their service are generally void and unenforceable. While restrictions during active employment are valid, post-employment restraints like this one are typically considered an unlawful restraint of trade unless they fall under very specific exceptions (like the sale of goodwill), which do not apply to standard employment contracts.
recommended_action: Remove this clause entirely or consult a lawyer to see if it can be narrowed significantly, as it is likely unenforceable and could create unnecessary legal ambiguity.
consequence: the clause is likely void and unenforceable, but its presence may be used to harass you or create legal disputes after you leave

plain_explanation: Any inventions, code, designs, or patentable work you create while working for the company and using its resources will belong entirely to the company. You will not own these creations personally.

Under Indian law, when work is created in the course of employment, the employer is generally considered the first owner of the copyright, or the employee assigns these rights to the employer. This clause explicitly confirms that ownership transfers to the company for work done during employment using company resources, which is a standard and lawful practice.
recommended_action: Nothing to do; this is standard.

plain_explanation: You agree to give the company ownership of any ideas or inventions you create, even if you make them in your own free time or for personal projects. This rule continues to apply for five years after you leave the job.
legal_assessment: This clause is likely unenforceable because it attempts to restrain you from using or benefiting from your own intellectual property created outside of work and after your employment has ended. Under Indian law, agreements that restrain a person from exercising a lawful profession or business are generally void. While assigning IP created during employment for company business is standard, extending this to personal time and post-employment acts as an unlawful restraint on trade.
recommended_action: Negotiate to remove the clause or limit it strictly to inventions created during working hours using company resources. Do not sign the contract as is, as it claims ownership of your personal creative work for years after you leave.
consequence: the company could claim ownership of your personal inventions and ideas for five years after you quit

cited_sources.text:
Agreement in restraint of trade, void.—Every agreement by which any one is restrained from
exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void.
_Exception_ 1.—Saving of agreement not to carry on business of which good-will is sold.—One
who sells the good-will of a business may agree with the buyer to refrain from carrying on a similar business, within specified local limits, so long as the buyer, or any person deriving title to the good-will from him, carries on a like business therein, provided that such limits appear to the Court reasonable, regard being had to the nature of the business.

plain_explanation: After you finish your probation period, you will get 18 days of paid vacation leave and 12 days of sick or casual leave each year. These days are paid, meaning you still receive your salary while taking them.
legal_assessment: This clause specifies standard leave entitlements (18 days privilege leave and 12 days sick/casual leave) which are common in Indian employment contracts. The provided statutory sources (Industrial Relations Code Sections 29 and 30) relate to the procedural framework for standing orders in industrial establishments and do not directly govern or restrict the specific number of leave days in a private employment contract. Therefore, no specific legal violation or enforceability issue arises from the text of this clause based on the retrieved sources. It is a standard, balanced term.
recommended_action: Nothing to do; this is a standard leave provision. You may want to confirm if these days reset every calendar year or roll over, but the clause itself is clear.

plain_explanation: If you quit your job before working for the company for 10 years, you will lose all the retirement savings (gratuity) you have earned. The company says it has the right to take this money away without any conditions.
legal_assessment: This clause is likely unenforceable because it attempts to waive a statutory right. Gratuity is a legal entitlement under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, which generally requires only 5 years of continuous service to be eligible. A contract cannot override this statutory minimum. Furthermore, under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, a clause that acts as a penalty (forfeiting the entire amount regardless of actual loss) is not enforceable as written; the court would only award reasonable compensation, not the full forfeiture. Since the clause purports to take away a right guaranteed by law regardless of the contract, it is classified as red.
recommended_action: Remove this clause entirely, as it is illegal. If the company insists on a retention policy, ask for it to be replaced with a standard 'clawback' provision that only recovers the specific bonus or incentive paid, not the statutory gratuity.
consequence: you could lose your legally mandated retirement savings if you leave before 10 years

legal_assessment: The clause requires a security deposit of ten months' rent, which exceeds the statutory limit for residential premises. Under the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, the maximum security deposit for a residential property is two months' rent. Therefore, this clause is likely unenforceable to the extent it demands more than the legal cap.

consequence: you may be forced to pay an illegal, excessive deposit that is hard to recover

plain_explanation: The landlord can increase your monthly rent if they give you 15 days' written notice. There is no limit mentioned on how much the rent can go up.
legal_assessment: This clause allows the landlord to revise rent with only 15 days' notice. Under the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, if the agreement does not specify a different notice period, the landlord must provide at least three months' notice before revising rent. A 15-day notice period is significantly shorter than the statutory minimum and likely unenforceable. Additionally, the clause does not cap the increase, which could allow for arbitrary or excessive hikes.
recommended_action: Negotiate to increase the notice period to at least three months, as required by the Model Tenancy Act. Also, ask to add a cap on the annual rent increase (e.g., 5-10%) to prevent arbitrary hikes.
consequence: the landlord can raise your rent significantly with only 15 days' warning

legal_assessment: The clause allows either party to terminate the tenancy with one month's written notice. This is a standard and balanced term for a monthly tenancy. Under the Transfer of Property Act, in the absence of a specific written contract, a monthly tenancy is typically terminable by 15 days' notice. However, parties are free to contractually agree to a longer notice period, such as one month, which is common and enforceable. The clause does not appear to be one-sided or unlawful.
recommended_action: Nothing to do; this is a standard and fair notice period for a monthly tenancy.

plain_explanation: You cannot end this rental agreement before 24 months have passed, even if your situation changes or you want to move out early. This rule applies no matter what happens.
legal_assessment: This clause imposes a rigid 24-month lock-in period that prevents termination regardless of circumstances. Under the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, while parties can agree on lock-in periods, a restriction that is unconscionable or one-sided, such as a 24-month ban on termination 'regardless of circumstances,' is likely to be viewed as an unreasonable restraint. The law generally allows termination by notice as agreed, but such an absolute and long-term restriction may be unenforceable or considered void as it takes away the tenant's right to exit the tenancy in a fair manner.
recommended_action: Negotiate to reduce the lock-in period to a more standard duration, such as 6 or 12 months, and ensure the clause allows for termination in case of force majeure or if the landlord breaches the agreement.
consequence: you could be legally bound to pay rent for the full 24 months even if you move out early

This aligns with the Model Tenancy Act's framework, which permits parties to agree on notice periods and lock-in restrictions. Since the clause is mutual and does not impose excessive burdens or void restraints, it is considered a fair and enforceable term.
recommended_action: Nothing to do; this is a standard and fair clause. Ensure you are comfortable with the 6-month commitment before signing.

legal_assessment: This clause allows the landlord to evict you through 'self-help' (changing locks or removing belongings) without following legal procedures. consequence: the landlord can lock you out or remove your belongings without going to court

legal_assessment: This clause establishes a pre-agreed, modest annual rent increase of 5%. Under the Model Tenancy Act, parties are free to agree on terms for rent revision. Since the increase is fixed, reasonable, and agreed upon in advance, it is a standard and lawful provision that does not violate statutory requirements for notice or arbitrary hikes.

plain_explanation: Your landlord can raise your rent by half at any time during the lease if they believe local property prices have gone up. This increase does not require a specific schedule or a fixed limit other than the 50% cap.
legal_assessment: This clause allows for an arbitrary and unilateral mid-term rent hike, which is generally considered unconscionable and one-sided. Under the Model Tenancy Act, rent revisions are typically governed by specific agreements or, in the absence of such agreements, require at least three months' notice. A clause permitting a 50% increase 'at any time' without a defined timeline or objective metric for 'market rates' creates significant legal uncertainty and likely violates the principle of fair dealing and statutory notice requirements for rent revision.

In that case, neither side can be blamed or punished for not finishing their part of the deal.

It aligns with Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which states that a contract becomes void if performance becomes impossible due to an event the promisor could not prevent. The clause is balanced as it applies to both parties and does not waive any statutory rights or impose unreasonable restrictions.
recommended_action: Nothing to do; this is a standard and fair clause.

cited_sources.title: Agreement to do impossible act
cited_sources.text:
Agreement to do impossible act.—An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void.
Contract to do an act afterwards becoming impossible or unlawful.—A contract to do an act
which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible, or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful.[1]
Compensation for loss through non-performance of act known to be impossible or unlawful.—
Where one person has promised to do something which he knew, or, with reasonable diligence, might have known, and which the promisee did not know, to be impossible or unlawful, such promisor must make compensation to such promisee for any loss which such promisee sustains through the nonperformance of the promise.
_Illustrations_
(a) A agrees with B to discover treasure by magic. The agreement is void.
(b) A and B contract to marry each other. Before the time fixed for the marriage, A goes mad. The contract becomes void.
(c) A contracts to marry B, being already married to C, and being forbidden by the law to which he is subject to practise
polygamy, A must make compensation to B for the loss caused to her by the non-performance of his promise.
(d) A contracts to take in cargo for B at a foreign port. A’s Government afterwards declares war against the country in which
the port is situated. The contract becomes void when war is declared.
(e) A contracts to act at a theatre for six months in consideration of a sum paid in advance by B. On several occasions A is
too ill to act. The contract to act on those occasions becomes void.

plain_explanation: You agree to give up your right to take the company to court or a labor tribunal if they fire you unfairly or do not pay your wages. This waiver applies to all such claims.
legal_assessment: This clause is likely void and unenforceable under Indian law. Section 28 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, explicitly states that any agreement which obstructs the right of a party to enforce their rights in a court of law is void to that extent. While Section 27 (restraint of trade) was retrieved, the specific legal principle governing the waiver of the right to approach a judicial forum is found in Section 28. Waiving the right to seek statutory dues or judicial remedy for wrongful termination is a fundamental breach of due process and cannot be contracted away.
recommended_action: Remove this clause entirely from the contract. Do not sign the agreement while it contains this waiver, as it attempts to illegally strip you of your legal rights.
consequence: the company could refuse to pay you or deny you legal recourse, and you might be unable to sue them for unpaid wages or wrongful termination

plain_explanation: If you and the other party have a disagreement about this contract, you must resolve it through a private legal process called arbitration instead of going to a public court. This process will take place in New Delhi and the decision made by the arbitrator will be final and binding on both sides.
legal_assessment: The clause mandates binding arbitration in New Delhi under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. While arbitration is a valid and common method for dispute resolution, this clause is one-sided if the parties are not based in New Delhi, as it forces the employee or tenant to travel to a specific city for legal proceedings. Additionally, binding arbitration generally waives the right to appeal the decision in a court of law, which can be disadvantageous if the arbitrator makes an error. The clause is lawful but may be inconvenient or costly for the individual.
recommended_action: If you do not live or work in New Delhi, ask to change the arbitration location to a city closer to you or to your workplace. If you cannot change the location, be aware that you will have to travel to New Delhi for any legal disputes and that the arbitrator's decision will be final.
consequence: you may have to travel to New Delhi to resolve disputes and lose the right to appeal the decision in a court

plain_explanation: If you have a problem with the company, you must first talk to their internal ombudsperson (a person appointed to handle complaints). You cannot start formal legal or negotiation talks until you have gone through this internal step.
legal_assessment: This clause imposes a mandatory internal dispute resolution step before any formal proceedings. While not explicitly void, it may be considered one-sided or an unreasonable delay if the internal process is not independent or if it effectively prevents you from seeking timely redress. The provided statute (Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 7) defines arbitration agreements but does not specifically address internal ombudsperson clauses; however, such clauses are often scrutinized for fairness and potential delay of statutory rights.

legal_assessment: This clause requires the employee to act in the company's best interests during employment. Under Indian law, an agreement that restrains a person from exercising a lawful profession or trade is void, but this restriction applies only to restraints that operate after employment ends. Restrictions on loyalty and conduct during active employment are standard and valid. Therefore, this clause is lawful and does not violate Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act.

legal_assessment: This is a standard clause allowing the employer to recover the cost of the notice period not served by deducting it from the employee's final dues. Under Indian law, specifically Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, parties are entitled to reasonable compensation for breach of contract. Since the notice period represents a specific, pre-agreed obligation, deducting the equivalent value from the final settlement is a common and generally enforceable method of calculating this compensation, provided it does not exceed the actual loss or the stipulated amount. It is not considered an unlawful penalty because it directly offsets the employer's loss of labor during the notice period.

cited_sources.text:
Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for.—[1][When a contract has
been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
_Explanation.—A stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a stipulation by_
way of penalty.]
_Exception.—When any person enters into any bail-bond, recognizance or other instrument of the_
same nature, or, under the provisions of any law, or under the orders of the [2][Central Government] or of any [3][State Government], gives any bond for the performance of any public duty or act in which the public are interested, he shall be liable, upon breach of the condition of any such instrument, to pay the whole sum mentioned therein.
_Explanation.—A person who enters into a contract with Government does not necessarily thereby_
undertake any public duty, or promise to do an act in which the public are interested.
_Illustrations_
(a)A contracts with B to pay B Rs. 1,000, if he fails to pay B Rs. 500 on a given day. A fails to pay B Rs. 500 on that day. B
is entitled to recover from A such compensation, not exceeding Rs. 1,000, as the Court considers reasonable.
(b)A contracts with B that, if Apractises as a surgeon within Calcutta, he will pay B Rs. 5,000. A practises as a surgeon in
Calcutta. B is entitled to such compensation; not exceeding Rs. 5,000, as the Court considers reasonable.
(c)A gives a recognizance binding him in a penalty of Rs. 500 to appear in Court on a certain day. He forfeits his
recognizance. He is liable to pay the whole penalty.

3. Subs. by the A.O. 1950, for “Provincial Government”.

(e) A, who owes money to B a money-lender, undertakes to repay him by delivering to him 10 maunds of grain on a certain
date, and stipulates that, in the event of his not delivering the stipulated amount by the stipulated date, he shall be liable to deliver

(f) A undertakes to repay B a loan of Rs. 1,000 by five equal monthly instalments, with a stipulation that in default of

(g) A borrows Rs. 100 from B and gives him a bond for Rs. 200 payable by five yearly instalments of Rs. 40, with a
stipulation that, in default of payment of any instalment, the whole shall become due. This is a stipulation by way of penalty.]

plain_explanation: If you move out before the one-year lock-in period ends, you will lose your security deposit. The contract calls this lost deposit a pre-agreed amount for damages.
legal_assessment: The clause imposes a financial penalty for early termination during the lock-in period. While lock-in periods are generally enforceable if agreed upon by both parties, the specific mechanism of forfeiting the entire security deposit as 'liquidated damages' requires scrutiny. Under Indian contract law, if a sum is named as a penalty, the court may award reasonable compensation not exceeding that amount, provided it is not unconscionable. The enforceability depends on whether the loss of the deposit is a genuine pre-estimate of the landlord's loss or an excessive penalty. Since the deposit is typically meant to secure performance and not to punish early exit, its total forfeiture for a breach of the lock-in period may be challenged as a penalty if it exceeds the actual loss suffered by the landlord.
recommended_action: Negotiate to clarify that the security deposit will be returned after deducting any actual damages or unpaid rent, rather than being fully forfeited. Alternatively, ask for a specific, reasonable early termination fee that is separate from the security deposit.
consequence: you could lose your entire security deposit if you leave early

cited_sources.jurisdiction: Model Act (applies only where adopted by a state)

legal_assessment: This is a standard and lawful provision. It ensures the employee is paid for the notice period while preventing them from accessing sensitive company data or disrupting operations during the transition. There are no legal issues with this clause as it protects both parties and complies with standard employment practices.

legal_assessment: The clause mandates a fixed deduction regardless of the actual condition of the property. While the Model Tenancy Act allows landlords to make deductions for tenant liabilities, it does not explicitly validate automatic, condition-independent charges. Such a clause is one-sided and potentially unfair because it penalizes the tenant even if the property was left in good condition. It may be challenged as an unreasonable penalty or a breach of the principle that deductions should reflect actual liability or damage.
recommended_action: Negotiate to remove the 'regardless of premises condition' wording. Instead, agree that painting and cleaning charges will only be deducted if the property is left in a condition worse than when you moved in, or if specific damage is documented.

legal_assessment: This clause is a standard pro-rata recovery of actual expenses (relocation allowance) upon early resignation. Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, such arrangements are generally enforceable as they represent a genuine pre-estimate of loss rather than a penalty, provided the amount recovered does not exceed the actual benefit received or the loss incurred. Since the refund is calculated pro-rata (in proportion to the time served), it aligns with the legal principle of recovering reasonable compensation for breach rather than imposing a punitive penalty.
recommended_action: Nothing to do; this is a standard and fair clause. Ensure you keep records of the relocation expenses if you plan to leave within the first year to verify the pro-rata calculation.

plain_explanation: If you do not pay your rent by the 5th of the month, you must pay an extra fee of Rs 1,000 for every day the payment is late. This fee keeps adding up until you pay the full amount.
legal_assessment: The clause imposes a fixed daily penalty of Rs 1,000 for late rent. recommended_action: Negotiate to remove the fixed daily penalty and replace it with a reasonable interest rate on the overdue amount, or a one-time modest late fee that reflects the actual inconvenience.
consequence: you could be forced to pay thousands of rupees in extra fees for a short delay, far more than the actual loss to the landlord
